newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU joins world debate on animal cloning.
newsitem.headline: EU joins world debate on animal cloning.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer joined the furore over sheep cloning on Thursday, ordering his specialists to investigate whether the European Union should take a stance on the issue.
The EU executive said Santer had ordered officials to investigate "if and to what extent" the EU should get involved.
But swift action did not seem likely after a noncommittal response from Commission spokesman Joao Vale de Almeida on the Commission's next step.

"The scope of the inquiry...is to see in which area there is Community competence (legal power). I did not say we were going to do something, I said we were going to study it," he told a news conference.

Concern about the ethical issues posed by the new technology has grown following the successful cloning of an adult sheep by scientists in Scotland working with the biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics plc.
The researchers who accomplished that feat admit it could now become possible to clone a human being, although they denounced anyone who would try.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has ordered the U.S. National Bioethics Advisory Panel to report within 90 days on the legal and ethical ramifications of cloning, especially its implications for humans.
Santer said he had asked the EU's Group of Advisers on the Ethical Implications of Biotechnology -- comprising outside scientists and legal and ethical experts -- to look at cloning.
"The Commission will examine the overall question in the light of the results of these different steps and in the framework of its specific competences," the statement said.
The EU has been embroiled in several high-profile rows over ethical questions related to genetic engineering.
An attempt to adopt legislation on biotechnology inventions was bogged down for years by debate over the propriety of issuing patents for genetically modified plants and animals.
The European Parliament threw out the first version of the text, forcing the Commission to redraft the rules to take more account of ethical concerns.
Similar disarray surrounded EU scrutiny of a French application to clear EU imports of Ciba Geigy's genetically modified maize for sale and cultivation.

Although the Commission cleared the maize last December, mounting confusion surrounds the issue now that Austria and Luxembourg have announced plans for national bans and France itself, the original applicant for clearance, banned cultivation of the maize during this year's harvest.

Both the European Commission and national governments acting at EU level have come under fire for their handling of the ethical, environmental and commercial questions raised by gene-manipulation technologies.
Critics say convoluted and contradictory legal procedures governing EU scientific committees, ministerial and executive meetings have led to widespread confusion about where the EU stands.
Santer, citing public concern, has pledged to review EU decision-making procedures in this area.
Several members of the European parliament's environment committee expressed concern about cloning on Thursday and called for tougher national and international policing of experiments.

"Cloning breaks new ethical ground, a fact which may deeply disturb and frighten many people," committee chairman Ken Collins said in a statement. "To answer these fears, we need to ensure that the benefits of genetic manipulation technology are not lost in a tidal wave of abuses."

The committee's Socialist spokeswoman, Dagmar Roth-Behrendt of Germany, said the World Trade Organisation should impose a global moratorium on cloning and set up an ethical committee to consider such questions.
